claims.text: The protective coating has a dual-phase microstructure containing distinct FCC and BCC regions.
The FCC and BCC regions form a network of heterophase boundaries under the standard processing route.
Changing annealing or quenching parameters can refine or coarsen the distribution and spacing of FCC/BCC heterophase interfaces.
FCC/BCC heterophase interfaces are the structural mediator governing the proposed creep resistance.
FCC/BCC heterophase boundaries act as physical obstacles that pin dislocations.
Heterophase boundaries increase the energy barrier for dislocation glide.
Heterophase boundaries increase the energy barrier for dislocation climb.
Impeded dislocation glide and climb delay the accumulation of creep deformation during continuous loading.
A refined and uniformly distributed heterophase-interface network will produce a lower creep strain rate than a coarser or less uniform interface network.
The proposed interface-pinning mechanism applies in temperature and stress regimes dominated by dislocation-mediated creep.
At very high temperatures or extreme stresses, grain-boundary sliding may become prevalent.
The creep-resistance contribution of heterophase-interface pinning may diminish when competing deformation mechanisms become prevalent.
The magnitude of the interface-pinning contribution relative to other creep-resistance mechanisms is not established.
Failure of refined-interface coatings to show a reproducibly lower creep strain rate than coarser-interface coatings under identical conditions would falsify the proposed primary mechanism.
